Top Takeaways for Clinicians from the KDIGO 2024
Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management
10 of ANCA-Associated Vasculitis (AAV)
Diagnosis of ANCA-associated vasculitis
Suspected kidney vasculitis
Diagnosis of AAV must be made as early as possible to decrease the risk of permanent
loss of kidney function and life-threatening complications. In case of clinical presenta-
tion compatible with small-vessel vasculitis in combination with positive myeloperoxi-
dase (MPO)- or proteinase 3 (PR3)-ANCA serology, waiting for kidney biopsy should
1 not delay starting immunosuppressive treatment, especially in patients who are Clinical presentation compatible Clinical presentation compatible
rapidly deteriorating (Figure 1). with ANCA vasculitis with any primary
PR3– or MPO–ANCA positive small-vessel vasculitis
Low suspicion for PR3– and MPO–ANCA negative
secondary vasculitis
Initial treatment
Initial treatment of AAV is glucocorticoids in combination with cyclophos-
phamide or rituximab (Figure 2). In patients with markedly reduced or
rapidly declining kidney function, both cyclophosphamide and glucocor-
ticoids, and the combination of rituximab and cyclophosphamide can be
2 Experienced center and No biopsy contraindication
considered in this setting. rapidly progressive disease

greater GFR recovery.
Plasma exchange Rituximab preferred Cyclophosphamide preferred
Plasma exchange should be considered for patients with SCr >3.4 mg/dl
• Children and adolescents • Rituximab difficult to access
• Pre-menopausal women and men • Severe GN (SCr >4 mg/dl
in patients with diffuse alveolar hemorrhage who have hypoxemia
4 (300 μmol/l), patients requiring dialysis or with rapidly increasing SCr, or
concerned about their fertility [354 μmol/l])*
(Figure 3). Plasma exchange should be added to initial treatment for
• Frail older adults

• Glucocorticoid-sparing especially
important
• Relapsing disease
• PR3–ANCA disease

A combination of 2 intravenous pulses of cyclophosphamide with rituximab
can be considered.
